verdict.summary:
# Draft clinical evidence summary — Tuberculin skin test (TST): when the reaction must be examined, and who must examine it

**Status: draft for review by a qualified clinician. This is not medical advice and is not for patient care. Every clinical statement below is tied to a quoted CDC source cited in full; where CDC is silent or its own pages differ in wording, that is stated.**

## 1. Scope and questions

- **Ask 2 (when):** at what time after placement must the TST reaction be examined?
- **Ask 3 (who):** who is required to examine/read the reaction?

Scope: the CDC page named in the request — *Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis* (health care provider section) — as available on 2026-11-21. Companion CDC pages are cited only to confirm wording, to supply the measurement technique the primary page omits, and to record discrepancies. They are labelled as such.

## 2. Sources, in full, with version control

**Primary source (the page named in the request):**

1. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. *Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis.* For Health Care Providers. Division of Tuberculosis Elimination; National Center for HIV, Viral Hepatitis, STD, and Tuberculosis Prevention. Page date: Apr. 17, 2025. URL: https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/. Snapshot retrieved 2026-11-23T04:17:05Z; sha256 9095c1db7f3e (harness record).

**Supporting CDC sources (confirmation and discrepancy check):**

2. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. *Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test.* Page date: January 31, 2025. URL: https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/tuberculin-skin-test.html. Retrieved 2026-11-23T04:17:05Z; sha256 4aa43e3065d3.
3. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. *Clinical Overview of Latent Tuberculosis Infection.* Page date: April 17, 2025. URL: https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/clinical-overview/latent-tuberculosis-infection.html. Retrieved 2026-11-23T04:17:05Z; sha256 05915436f177.
4. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. *Tuberculin Skin Testing: Information for Health Care Providers* (fact sheet, PDF). URL: https://www.cdc.gov/tb/publications/factsheets/testing/Tuberculin_Skin_Testing_Information_for_Health_Care_Providers.pdf. Retrieved 2026-11-23T04:17:05Z; sha256 8e42decc7a4c. No page date is visible in the retrieved text.
5. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. *Testing for Tuberculosis: Skin Test* (patient-facing page). Page date: January 31, 2025. URL: https://www.cdc.gov/tb/testing/skin-test.html. Retrieved 2026-11-23T04:17:05Z; sha256 50e30e96219d.

**Version note (read before relying on the quotes).** The requested date is 2026-11-21; the snapshot was taken 2026-11-23T04:17:05Z, two days later. The primary page carries the date stamp “Apr. 17, 2025” and the TST subpage “January 31, 2025”, both earlier than 2026-11-21; any revision between 2026-11-21 and 2026-11-23 would have carried a newer stamp, and none appears. The content in force on 2026-11-21 is therefore the content quoted, as an inference from the page date stamps — not as a byte-level archive capture of 2026-11-21. If a capture of that exact date is required for a regulatory file, retrieve the archived copy (e.g., Internet Archive Wayback Machine) and re-verify the two key sentences quoted in §3.

## 3. Findings, verbatim

**Primary page [1], timing and reader:**

> “After 48–72 hours, the skin test reaction must be examined by a trained health care worker. The health care worker measures any swelling where the tuberculin was injected to determine if the reaction to the test is positive or negative.”

**Primary page [1], who may read:**

> “TB skin results should only be read by a trained health care professional. Consult with your state and local public health authorities to determine who is authorized to place and read TB skin tests in your state.”

**TST subpage [2], timing, reader, measurement and authorisation:**

> “The skin test reaction should be read between 48 and 72 hours after administration by a health care worker trained to read TB skin results.”
>
> “A patient who does not return within 72 hours will need to be rescheduled for another skin test.”
>
> “The TB skin test should be placed (administered) and read by a designated, trained health care provider. Consult with your state and local public health authorities to determine who is authorized to place and read TB skin tests in your state.”
>
> “The reaction should be measured in millimeters of the induration (firm swelling). The reader should not measure erythema (redness). The diameter of the indurated area should be measured across the forearm (perpendicular to the long axis).”

**LTBI clinical overview [3]:**

> “After 48–72 hours, the skin test reaction must be examined by a trained health care worker. The health care worker measures the induration (firm swelling) where the tuberculin was injected to determine if the reaction to the test is positive or negative.”

**PDF fact sheet [4]:**

> “The skin test reaction should be read between 48 and 72 hours after administration by a health care worker trained to read TST results. A patient who does not return within 72 hours will need to be rescheduled for another skin test.”
>
> Administration context: “the TST is performed by injecting 0.1 ml of tuberculin purified protein derivative (PPD) into the inner surface of the forearm … When placed correctly, the injection should produce a pale elevation of the skin (a wheal) 6 to 10 mm in diameter.”

**Patient-facing page [5]:**

> “After two or three days, you must return to the clinic to have the skin test read. A trained health care provider will measure the size of the bump or reaction.”

## 4. Answers

**Ask 2 — When must the TST reaction be examined?**
**48 to 72 hours after administration** (unit: hours after intradermal placement of 0.1 mL PPD). The reaction must be examined within that window; CDC's operational corollary is that a patient who does not return within 72 hours must be rescheduled for another skin test [2][4]. The window is identical across the primary page [1], the TST subpage [2], the LTBI overview [3] and the PDF fact sheet [4]; the patient page's “two or three days” [5] is the same window stated less precisely. CDC's primary page does not give a separate instruction for a reading taken before 48 hours — do not infer one from this page.

**Ask 3 — Who must examine it?**
**A trained health care worker** — the primary page's wording [1], which also states results “should only be read by a trained health care professional” [1]. Equivalently, on CDC's TST subpage and fact sheet: “a health care worker trained to read TB skin results” [2][4], and, for placement and reading together, “a designated, trained health care provider” [2]. In all CDC variants the reader must be **trained**; **which** trained persons are authorised to place and read is set by state and local public health authorities, and CDC expressly directs the reader to consult them [1][2]. No CDC source on these pages permits an untrained reader or patient self-reading.

**Technique that goes with the reading (from [2][4], not stated on the primary page):** the reaction is measured in **millimetres of induration** (firm swelling), **not** erythema (redness), with the diameter measured across the forearm perpendicular to the long axis.

## 5. Evidence quality, thin spots and conflicts

- **Evidence level.** The 48–72 hour window and the trained-reader requirement are CDC programmatic guidance from the Division of Tuberculosis Elimination [1–5]. The primary page cites no trial, systematic review or formal graded guideline for either element; it is guidance-level (standard-of-practice), not trial-level, evidence. This should be described that way in any downstream document.
- **Wording inconsistency, not substantive conflict.** “trained health care worker” [1][3], “trained health care professional” [1], “health care worker trained to read TB skin results” [2][4], “designated, trained health care provider” [2]. All variants require training; “designated” appears only in [2] and is the closest CDC comes to naming an appointment/authorisation process. No variant contradicts another on timing or on the training requirement.
- **Thin spot — measurement method.** The primary page [1] states only that the worker measures “any swelling”; the induration-not-erythema rule and the transverse-axis rule appear on the linked subpage [2] and the PDF [4]. If a downstream document must be confined strictly to the primary page, the measurement-technique statements fall outside that scope; the timing and reader statements do not.
- **Thin spot — the 48-hour lower bound.** CDC states the window's start but does not state what to do with a reading taken before 48 hours. No instruction is invented here.
- **Thin spot — authorisation.** CDC does not name which professions may read a TST; it delegates to state and local public health authorities [1][2]. Any statement that a specific profession (e.g., nurse, pharmacist, medical assistant) is or is not authorised is outside CDC's text.
- **Different test, different logistics.** Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) requires a single blood draw and no return visit for reading [4]; the 48–72 hour reading window applies to the TST only and must not be transferred to IGRA.
- **No numeric conflict.** The only figures in the timing rule are 48 h and 72 h; the rescheduling rule uses 72 h, the window's upper bound, and is consistent with it. TST interpretation cut-offs (5/10/15 mm induration, on [2]) are a separate question and are deliberately not used here.

## 6. Populations and circumstances CDC flags on these same pages (context only — not new answers)

- **Children younger than 5 years:** CDC guidelines recommend the TST as the testing method, noting some experts use IGRA; AAP guidance may be consulted [1].
- **BCG-vaccinated persons:** IGRA preferred, because BCG can cause a false-positive TST [3][4].
- **Persons unlikely to return for a reading:** IGRA preferred — a direct consequence of the mandatory 48–72 hour return [3].
- **Prior severe reaction to a TST:** contraindication to repeating the test [2].
- **Recent live-virus vaccination** (measles, mumps, rubella, oral polio, varicella, yellow fever, BCG, oral typhoid): TST either the same day or at least 1 month after [4].
- **Symptoms of TB disease:** do not wait for the TST result before starting other diagnostic tests [2].
- **Routine testing with both IGRA and TST is not recommended** [3].

## 7. Review checklist for the qualified clinician signing this off

1. Confirm “48–72 hours” is expressed in **hours after placement**, not days, and that the 72-hour upper bound matches the rescheduling rule quoted in §3.
2. Confirm the reader-qualification wording against your jurisdiction's public health regulations, since CDC defers authorisation to state and local authorities [1][2].
3. Confirm the measurement convention: millimetres of induration, transverse to the long axis of the forearm, erythema not measured [2][4].
4. Confirm the page version. If a byte-level capture dated 2026-11-21 is required, pull the archived copy and re-verify the two key sentences in §3 before the document is finalised.

findings.question:
1. Under 21 CFR Part 814 as in force on 2026-11-21, within how many days after FDA receives a PMA must FDA notify the applicant whether the application has been filed?

quotes.whole:
§ 814.40 Time frames for reviewing a PMA.


Within 180 days after receipt of an application that is accepted for filing and to which the applicant does not submit a major amendment, FDA will review the PMA and, after receiving the report and recommendation of the appropriate FDA advisory committee, send the applicant an approval order under § 814.44(d), an approvable letter under § 814.44(e), a not approvable letter under § 814.44(f), or an order denying approval under § 814.45. The approvable letter and the not approvable letter will provide an opportunity for the applicant to amend or withdraw the application, or to consider the letter to be a denial of approval of the PMA under § 814.45 and to request administrative review under section 515 (d)(4) and (g) of the act.


[51 FR 26364, July 22, 1986, as amended at 87 FR 2045, Jan. 13, 2022]

(g) All safety and effectiveness data and other information not previously disclosed to the public are available for public disclosure if any one of the following events occurs and the data and information do not constitute trade secret or confidential commercial or financial information under § 20.61:
(1) The PMA has been abandoned. FDA will consider a PMA abandoned if:

(ii) The applicant fails to communicate with FDA within 7 days after the date on which FDA notifies the applicant that the PMA appears to have been abandoned.
(2) An order denying approval of the PMA has issued, and all legal appeals have been exhausted.
(3) An order withdrawing approval of the PMA has issued, and all legal appeals have been exhausted.
(4) The device has been reclassified.
(5) The device has been found to be substantially equivalent to a class I or class II device.
(6) The PMA is considered voluntarily withdrawn under § 814.44(g).

§ 814.42 Filing a PMA.
(a) The filing of an application means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the application is sufficiently complete to permit a substantive review. Within 45 days after a PMA is received by FDA, the agency will notify the applicant whether the application has been filed.
(b) If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (e) of this section for refusing to file the PMA applies, the agency will file the PMA and will notify the applicant in writing of the filing. verdict.summary:
DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED REGULATORY/CLINICAL REVIEW — not legal advice, not medical advice, not for patient care.

=== ANSWER (ask 2) ===
45 days. Under 21 CFR 814.42(a), FDA must notify the applicant whether a PMA has been filed within 45 days after FDA receives the PMA. The 45 days are calendar days (basis in section 4 below).

=== 1. AUTHORITY, CITED IN FULL AND VERBATIM ===
21 CFR 814.42(a) — 'Filing a PMA', Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter H (Medical Devices), Part 814 (Premarket Approval of Medical Devices), Subpart C (FDA Action on a PMA). Verbatim text of paragraph (a):

  'The filing of an application means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the application is sufficiently complete to permit a substantive review. Within 45 days after a PMA is received by FDA, the agency will notify the applicant whether the application has been filed.'

Companion paragraphs of the same section, quoted verbatim because they fix what the 45-day notice must contain and what the notice triggers:
  814.42(b): 'If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (e) of this section for refusing to file the PMA applies, the agency will file the PMA and will notify the applicant in writing of the filing. The notice will include the PMA reference number and the date FDA filed the PMA. The date of filing is the date that a PMA accepted for filing was received by the agency. The 180-day period for review of a PMA starts on the date of filing.'
  814.42(c): 'If FDA refuses to file a PMA, the agency will notify the applicant of the reasons for the refusal. This notice will identify the deficiencies in the application that prevent filing and will include the PMA reference number.'

Source note printed at the end of §814.42 in the Code of Federal Regulations: '[51 FR 26364, July 22, 1986, as amended at 63 FR 5254, Feb. 2, 1998; 73 FR 49942, Aug. 25, 2008; 85 FR 18442, Apr. 2, 2020]'.

Sources used (all retrieved 2026-11-23, i.e. two days after the target date):
  (i) eCFR, 21 CFR Part 814, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-814 — fetched 2026-11-23T04:19:51Z, sha256 7c4288803759. Contains the quoted 814.42(a) sentence.
  (ii) GovInfo, CFR-2025-title21-vol8, part 814 XML, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol8/xml/CFR-2025-title21-vol8-part814.xml — fetched 2026-11-23T04:19:51Z, sha256 0aa9c4d303d5. Contains the identical 814.42(a) sentence and the source note.
  (iii) GovInfo, CFR-2025-title21-vol8, PDF sec814-40.pdf (which carries the §814.42 text on its following pages), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol8/pdf/CFR-2025-title21-vol8-sec814-40.pdf — fetched 2026-11-23T04:19:51Z, sha256 9b051c6f3b2e. Contains the identical 814.42(a) sentence.
  (iv) eCFR, section-level page, http://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-814/subpart-C/section-814.40 — fetched 2026-11-23T04:19:52Z, sha256 fc9ad46b5ac8.

=== 2. VERSION IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21 (ask 1) ===
Two independently published renderings agree word for word: the annual CFR edition with edition date 2025-04-01 (source ii/iii) and the eCFR 'current' text as fetched on 2026-11-23 (source i). The amendment history attached to §814.42 lists no amendment after 85 FR 18442 (Apr. 2, 2020), so no amendment to §814.42 took effect between the 2025 annual edition and 2026-11-23. The text therefore governs 2026-11-21.
Residual verification the reviewer should perform before the answer is relied on externally: a point-in-time eCFR query for 2026-11-21 (the harness fetched 'current' on 2026-11-23, not a dated snapshot), and a Federal Register search for any Part 814 document published between 2026-11-21 and the review date that changes §814.42. Absent such a document, 45 days is the answer.

=== 3. WHY 814.40 IS NOT THE ANSWER — CORRECTION OF THE WORKING ASSUMPTION ===
The working assumption in the project context nominated 21 CFR 814.40 as the filing-notification provision. That is incorrect and would produce the wrong number. Verbatim, §814.40 ('Time frames for reviewing a PMA') reads: 'Within 180 days after receipt of an application that is accepted for filing and to which the applicant does not submit a major amendment, FDA will review the PMA and, after receiving the report and recommendation of the appropriate FDA advisory committee, send the applicant an approval order under §814.44(d), an approvable letter under §814.44(e), a not approvable letter under §814.44(f), or an order denying approval under §814.45.' §814.40 contains no filing-notification deadline. 180 days is the substantive-review clock; 45 days (814.42(a)) is the filing-notification clock. The two are sequential, not alternatives: the 180-day clock starts on the date of filing (814.42(b)), and the date of filing is the date FDA received a PMA that it accepted for filing (814.42(b)).

=== 4. 'DAYS' = CALENDAR DAYS ===
§814.42(a) says '45 days' with no qualifier. Part 814 uses the explicit term 'working days' when it means working days: §814.42(d)(2) requires a request for an informal conference 'within 10 working days of the date of receipt of the notice refusing to file the PMA', provides that 'FDA will hold the informal conference within 10 working days of its receipt of the request', and that FDA 'will render its decision on filing within 5 working days after the informal conference'. Because the same section distinguishes 'working days' from unqualified 'days', the 45 days in paragraph (a) are calendar days. Note the practical consequence the reviewer should flag to sponsors: if FDA refuses to file, the informal-conference route runs on working-day periods inside a decision process that is separate from the 45-day notification duty.

=== 5. SCOPE — WHAT THE 45-DAY FIGURE COVERS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT ===
Covered: an original PMA received by FDA. The text says 'a PMA' and sits in Subpart C, which governs FDA action on a PMA.
Not covered by this figure, and not to be quoted as if it were:
  - Humanitarian Device Exemptions: §814.112(a) provides a 30-day filing notification ('Within 30 days from the date an HDE is received by FDA, the agency will notify the applicant whether the application has been filed'), and §814.114 provides a 75-day decision clock for an HDE accepted for filing. Different subpart, different numbers.
  - PMA supplements: the retrieved passages do not state a separate filing-notification period for supplements. Whether §814.42(a) applies directly to a supplement, or whether supplement filing is handled under §814.39, was not established from the retrieved text and must be verified against §814.39 before the 45-day figure is applied to a supplement.
  - Modular PMAs: not addressed in the retrieved passages; verify against current FDA guidance before applying.
  - The 180-day review clock and its extension: a major amendment may extend the review period up to 180 days, and the review period may be extended by the days elapsing between an FDA request for a major amendment and receipt of a written decline. These affect the review clock, not the 45-day filing notification.

=== 6. HOW TO STATE IT IN A SUBMISSION OR MEMO ===
'Under 21 CFR 814.42(a) (text as published in the 2025 annual edition of 21 CFR chapter I subchapter H part 814 and unchanged in the eCFR current text as of 23 November 2026; last amended at 85 FR 18442, 2 April 2020), FDA must notify the applicant within 45 days after FDA receives a PMA whether the application has been filed. Under 21 CFR 814.42(b), the date of filing is the date FDA received a PMA accepted for filing, and the 180-day review period under 21 CFR 814.40 runs from that date.'

=== 7. REVIEWER SIGN-OFF CHECKLIST ===
[ ] Point-in-time eCFR snapshot for 2026-11-21 confirms §814.42(a) reads '45 days'.
[ ] No Federal Register document affecting §814.42 published between 2026-11-21 and the reliance date.
[ ] Scope of the statement confirmed (original PMA only, or supplement/modular position separately verified).
[ ] 'Calendar days' reading accepted for the document's purpose.

This is a regulatory-citation answer for a qualified reviewer; it is not legal advice, not medical advice, and not for patient care.

§ 820.7 Incorporation by reference.

quotes.whole:
The FDA issued the Medical Devices; Quality System Regulation Amendments Final Rule to amend the device CGMP requirements of 21 CFR part 820 to harmonize and modernize the regulation. The FDA is incorporating by reference the international standard specific for medical device quality management systems set by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), ISO 13485:2016 Medical devices – Quality management systems – Requirements for regulatory purposes.
The rule is effective February 2, 2026, and is now titled Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR).
Applicability of the QMSR
The QMSR regulation applies to finished device manufacturers who intend to commercially distribute medical devices. A finished device is defined in 21 CFR 820.3(a) as any device or accessory to any device that is suitable for use or capable of functioning, whether or not it is packaged, labeled, or sterilized.
Certain components such as blood tubing and diagnostic x-ray components are considered by the FDA to be finished devices because they are accessories to finished devices. A manufacturer of accessories is subject to the QMSR.

quotes.whole:
The QMSR incorporates by reference the international standard, ISO 13485:2016, Medical devices - Quality management systems - Requirements for regulatory purposes and clause 3 of ISO 9000:2015, Quality management systems - Fundamentals and vocabulary. This allows U.S. medical device quality management system requirements to align with internationally recognized standards and reduce burden on regulated industry.
Incorporating by reference ISO 13485:2016 as the foundational quality management system framework for medical device manufacturers promotes consistency in design, production, and lifecycle controls across global markets and now specifically requires risk management.
Incorporating by reference the terms and definitions set forth in Clause 3 of ISO 9000:2015 supports a common understanding of quality management system fundamentals. However, to the extent any clause of ISO 13485 conflicts with any provision of the FD&C Act and its implementing regulations, the FD&C Act and/or its implementing regulations will control. This ensures that public health protections, regulatory expectations, and enforcement authorities under the FD&C Act remain fully intact.

quotes.whole:
§ 820.3 Definitions.


The definitions in ISO 13485 and in Clause 3 of ISO 9000 (incorporated by reference, see § 820.7) apply to this part, except as specified in paragraph (b) of this section, and do not affect the meaning of similar terms defined in this title.




(a) The following terms, which are either not used or not defined in ISO 13485 or in Clause 3 of ISO 9000, also apply for the purposes of this part:




Batch or lot   means one or more components or finished devices that consist of a single type, model, class, size, composition, or software version that are manufactured under essentially the same conditions and that are intended to have uniform characteristics and quality within specified limits.






Component   means any raw material, substance, piece, part, software, firmware, labeling, or assembly that is intended to be included as part of the finished, packaged, and labeled device.






Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act   means the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, 21 U.S.C. 321 et seq., as amended.






Finished device   means any device or accessory to any device that is suitable for use or capable of functioning, whether or not it is packaged, labeled, or sterilized.






Human cell, tissue, or cellular or tissue-based product (HCT/P) regulated as a device   means an HCT/P as defined in § 1271.3(d) of this chapter that does not meet the criteria in § 1271.10(a) of this chapter and that is also regulated as a device.






Remanufacturer   means any person who processes, conditions, renovates, repackages, restores, or does any other act to a finished device that significantly changes the finished device's performance or safety specifications, or intended use.








(b) All definitions in section 201 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act shall apply to the regulation of quality management systems under this part and shall supersede the correlating terms and definitions in ISO 13485 (e.g., the definitions of device and labeling in section 201(h) and (m) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act apply to this part and supersede the definitions for the correlating terms in ISO 13485 (labelling and medical device)). In addition, the following terms and definitions apply to this part and supersede the definitions for the correlating terms in ISO 13485 or ISO 9000:




Implantable medical device  shall have the meaning of “implant” as defined in section 860.3 of this chapter.






Manufacturer  means any person who designs, manufactures, fabricates, assembles, or processes a finished device. Manufacturer includes, but is not limited to, those who perform the functions of contract sterilization, installation, relabeling, remanufacturing, repacking, or specification development, and initial distributors of foreign entities performing these functions.






Organization  shall have the meaning of “manufacturer” as defined in this part.






Rework  means action taken on a nonconforming product so that it will fulfill the specified requirements in the medical device file (MDF) before it is released for distribution.





Safety and Performance  shall have the meaning of “safety and effectiveness” in Clause 0.1 of ISO 13485. The phrase “safety and performance” does not relieve a manufacturer from any obligation to implement controls or other measures that provide reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness.





[89 FR 7523, Feb. 2, 2024; 89 FR 82945, Oct. 15, 2024]

verdict.summary:
Regulatory affairs answer (draft for qualified regulatory/quality reviewer; not medical advice).

1. Direct answer. As in force on 2026-11-21, 21 CFR Part 820 incorporates by reference ISO 13485:2016(E), Medical devices—Quality management systems—Requirements for regulatory purposes, Third edition, March 1, 2016. The edition is the Third edition; the ISO edition date is 2016-03-01 (March 1, 2016). It is not ISO 13485:2003.

2. Operative CFR text. 21 CFR 820.7(b) states: ISO 13485:2016(E) (“ISO 13485”), Medical devices—Quality management systems—Requirements for regulatory purposes, Third edition, March 1, 2016; IBR approved for §§ 820.1, 820.3, 820.10, 820.35, and 820.45. Source: 21 CFR 820.7, eCFR current text retrieved 2026-11-23T04:22:34Z, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-820/subpart-A/section-820.7, sha256 1d548e5e4598. The (E) suffix is part of the CFR designation and denotes the English-language edition as cited by FDA.

3. Why this is the text in force on 2026-11-21. The QMSR final rule, Medical Devices; Quality System Regulation Amendments, 89 FR 7523 (Feb. 2, 2024), amended 21 CFR Part 820 and became effective February 2, 2026. FDA’s QMSR page, updated February 2, 2026, states that the QMSR became effective on February 2, 2026, and that FDA is incorporating by reference ISO 13485:2016. The eCFR current text retrieved 2026-11-23T04:22:34Z still contains the § 820.7(b) IBR entry above and carries the source note [89 FR 7523, Feb. 2, 2024; 89 FR 82945, Oct. 15, 2024] at § 820.3. No later amendment appears in the retrieved text. Because 2026-11-21 falls after 2026-02-02 and before the 2026-11-23 retrieval, the answer is confirmed for the as-of date; for a formal file, save an eCFR point-in-time snapshot or PDF dated 2026-11-21. Note: the project-context citation 86 FR 73174 (Dec. 10, 2021) is not the QMSR final rule; the final rule citation is 89 FR 7523 (Feb. 2, 2024).

4. Manual correction. Replace the legacy citation ISO 13485:2003 with: ISO 13485:2016(E), Medical devices—Quality management systems—Requirements for regulatory purposes, Third edition, March 1, 2016, as incorporated by reference at 21 CFR 820.7(b) (Quality Management System Regulation, effective February 2, 2026). Add the Part 820 qualifier: compliance with ISO 13485 is not alone sufficient; 21 CFR 820.10(a) requires a documented QMS that complies with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485 and other applicable requirements of Part 820, and FDA-specific provisions add to or supersede the ISO text (for example, 21 CFR 820.3 definitions; 21 CFR 820.10(b)(1) UDI for Clause 7.5.8; 21 CFR 820.45 labeling and packaging controls in addition to Clause 7.5.1). Do not write that FDA adopts ISO 13485 verbatim. The old QSR did not incorporate ISO 13485; the 2003 citation was not an FDA IBR requirement under the pre-2026 Part 820. If the organization’s ISO certificate or EU MDR/Health Canada file cites a different edition or an ISO amendment, keep that as a separate market-specific citation; the U.S. Part 820 citation remains the Third edition, March 1, 2016, named in § 820.7(b).

5. Sources cited in full.
- 21 CFR 820.7, Incorporation by reference, eCFR, Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter H, Part 820, Subpart A, current text retrieved 2026-11-23T04:22:34Z, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-820/subpart-A/section-820.7, sha256 1d548e5e4598.

- 21 CFR 820.3, Definitions, eCFR, Part 820, Subpart B, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-820/subpart-B/section-820.3, sha256 88bcd7a5b56e.
- U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR), updated February 2, 2026, https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/postmarket-requirements-devices/quality-management-system-regulation-qmsr, sha256 5084a62b61b9.
- Medical Devices; Quality System Regulation Amendments, final rule, 89 FR 7523 (Feb. 2, 2024), https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/02/02/2024-01709/medical-devices-quality-system-regulation-amendments.

6. Result statement for the requested value. The identifier is ISO 13485:2016(E), Third edition, March 1, 2016. Unit: not applicable (identifier).

quotes.whole:
Editorial Note on Part 860




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 860 appear at 73 FR 35341, June 23, 2008, and at 86 FR 54846, Oct. 5, 2021.






§ 860.230 Accepting a De Novo request.




(a) The acceptance of a De Novo request means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the De Novo request contains the information necessary to permit a substantive review. Within 15 days after a De Novo request is received by FDA, FDA will notify the requester whether the De Novo request has been accepted.






(b) If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (c)(1) of this section for refusing to accept the De Novo request apply or FDA fails to complete the acceptance review within 15 days, FDA will accept the De Novo request for review and will notify the requester. The notice will include the De Novo request reference number and the date FDA accepted the De Novo request. The date of acceptance is the date that an accepted De Novo request was received by FDA.






(c) 




(1) FDA may refuse to accept a De Novo request if any of the following applies:




(i) The requester has an open or pending premarket submission or reclassification petition for the device;






(ii) The De Novo request is incomplete because it does not on its face contain all the information required under section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or does not contain each of the items required under this part, or a justification for omission of any item;






(iii) The De Novo request is not formatted as required under § 860.210;






(iv) The De Novo request is for multiple devices and those devices are of more than one type; or






(v) The requester has not responded to, or has failed to provide a rationale for not responding to, deficiencies identified by FDA in previous submissions for the same device, including those submissions described in § 860.220(a)(3).








(2) If FDA refuses to accept a De Novo request, FDA will notify the requester of the reasons for the refusal. The notice will identify the deficiencies in the De Novo request that prevent accepting and will include the De Novo request reference number.





(3) If FDA refuses to accept a De Novo request, the requester may submit the additional information necessary to comply with the requirements of section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and this part. The additional information must include the De Novo request reference number of the original submission. If the De Novo request is subsequently accepted, the date of acceptance is the date FDA receives the additional information.

quotes.whole:
Editorial Note on Part 860




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 860 appear at 73 FR 35341, June 23, 2008, and at 86 FR 54846, Oct. 5, 2021.






§ 860.240 Procedures for review of a De Novo request.




(a) FDA will begin substantive review of a De Novo request after the De Novo request is accepted under § 860.230. Within 120 days after receipt of a De Novo request or receipt of additional information that results in the De Novo request being accepted under § 860.230, FDA will review the De Novo request and send the requester an order granting the De Novo request under § 860.260(a) or an order declining the De Novo request under 860.260(b).






(b) A requester may supplement or amend a pending De Novo request to revise existing information or provide additional information.




(1) FDA may require additional information regarding the device that is necessary for FDA to complete the review of the De Novo request.






(2) Additional information submitted to FDA must include the reference number assigned to the original De Novo request and, if submitted on the requester's own initiative, the reason for submitting the additional information.








(c) Prior to granting or declining a De Novo request, FDA may inspect relevant facilities to help determine:




(1) That clinical or nonclinical data were collected in a manner that ensures that the data accurately represents the benefits and risks of the device; or





(2) That implementation of Quality Management System Regulation (part 820 of this chapter) requirements, in addition to other general controls and any specified special controls, provide adequate assurance that critical and/or novel manufacturing processes produce devices that meet specifications necessary to ensure reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness.





[86 FR 54847, Oct. 5, 2021, as amended at 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025]

verdict.summary:
DRAFT FOR REVIEW BY A QUALIFIED REGULATORY/CLINICAL REVIEWER. Not legal advice and not medical advice; not for use in patient care. Every figure below is tied to a cited provision.

====================================================================
0. QUESTION, POPULATION, EXPOSURE, UNITS
====================================================================
Question: FDA receives a De Novo request that is accepted without any additional-information submission. Under 21 CFR Part 860 as in force on 2026-11-21, what are the outside time limits (a) for FDA's acceptance notification and (b) for FDA's review and issuance of an order granting or declining the request?

- Population: De Novo classification requests for a single device type submitted under 21 CFR 860.200(b) (i.e., after a not-substantially-equivalent determination on a 510(k), or where the requester determines no legally marketed predicate exists).
- Exposure / scenario: a request that is complete at intake and is accepted with no additional-information submission and no acceptance-review interaction (no Refuse-to-Accept, no response to an RTA notification).
- Units: all figures are in days. Part 860 says 'days' without a business-day qualifier; FDA's acceptance-review guidance states the acceptance review is conducted 'within 15 calendar days' and that acceptance-review days 'are included within the calendar days to reach a final decision'. Accordingly all figures below are CALENDAR DAYS.

====================================================================
1. SHORT ANSWER
====================================================================
(a) Acceptance notification: OUTSIDE LIMIT = 15 calendar days after FDA receives the De Novo request. Source: 21 CFR 860.230(a) and (b).
(b) Review and order granting or declining: OUTSIDE LIMIT = 120 calendar days after receipt of the De Novo request (or after receipt of the additional information that results in acceptance under 860.230). Source: 21 CFR 860.240(a).

The 15-day acceptance notification is not additive to the 120 days: the acceptance-review period is contained within the 120-day period, so the outer limit for the order remains 120 calendar days from receipt of the request.

====================================================================
2. SOURCE VERSION CONTROL (as in force on 2026-11-21)
====================================================================
- Primary source: 21 CFR Part 860, Subpart D (De Novo Classification), as published in the eCFR (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/part-860 and section pages /section-860.230 and /section-860.240), fetched 2026-11-23T04:25:13Z.
- Corroborating source: 2025 edition of the CFR, Title 21, Volume 8, Part 860 Subpart D (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol8/xml/CFR-2025-title21-vol8-part860-subpartD.xml), fetched 2026-11-23T04:25:12Z — identical operative language for 860.230(a)/(b) and 860.240(a).
- Amendment history printed on 860.240: '[86 FR 54847, Oct. 5, 2021, as amended at 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025]'. The only amendment after the 2021 De Novo rule and before 2026-11-21 is the December 4, 2025 amendment, which appears in 860.240(c) (substitution of 'Quality Management System Regulation (part 820 of this chapter)' for the former device-quality-system reference). It does not touch the 15-day or 120-day figures in 860.230(a)/(b) or 860.240(a).
- Part-level nomenclature notes: 73 FR 35341 (June 23, 2008) and 86 FR 54846 (Oct. 5, 2021); neither alters the day counts.
- Residual version risk to be closed by the reviewer: the text was captured on 2026-11-23, i.e., two days AFTER the target date of 2026-11-21. A change effective 2026-11-22 or 2026-11-23 would not be excluded by this capture. Because the eCFR amendment line shows no amendment between 2025-12-04 and the capture, the probability of a discrepancy is low, but the reviewer should re-pull 860.230 and 860.240 against a date-specific eCFR point-in-time view for 2026-11-21 before the draft is finalised.

====================================================================
3. THE TWO LIMITS, WITH THE OPERATIVE TEXT
====================================================================
3.1 Acceptance notification — 15 calendar days
21 CFR 860.230(a): 'The acceptance of a De Novo request means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the De Novo request contains the information necessary to permit a substantive review. Within 15 days after a De Novo request is received by FDA, FDA will notify the requester whether the De Novo request has been accepted.'
21 CFR 860.230(b): 'If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (c)(1) of this section for refusing to accept the De Novo request apply or FDA fails to complete the acceptance review within 15 days, FDA will accept the De Novo request for review and will notify the requester. The notice will include the De Novo request reference number and the date FDA accepted the De Novo request. The date of acceptance is the date that an accepted De Novo request was received by FDA.'
Reading: 15 days from FDA RECEIPT (not from any later administrative step) is the outside limit for the notification, and the notification is due whether the outcome is acceptance or refusal. If FDA does not complete the acceptance review within those 15 days, 860.230(b) converts the request to accepted status and requires notification — the 15-day limit therefore cannot be cured by inaction.

3.2 Review and order granting or declining — 120 calendar days
21 CFR 860.240(a): 'FDA will begin substantive review of a De Novo request after the De Novo request is accepted under § 860.230. Within 120 days after receipt of a De Novo request or receipt of additional information that results in the De Novo request being accepted under § 860.230, FDA will review the De Novo request and send the requester an order granting the De Novo request under § 860.260(a) or an order declining the De Novo request under 860.260(b).'
Reading: the 120-day clock runs from RECEIPT OF THE REQUEST in the scenario at issue (a request accepted without any additional-information submission). The alternative start point ('receipt of additional information that results in the De Novo request being accepted') is not triggered here — it applies only where FDA initially refused to accept and the requester supplied corrective information under 860.230(c)(3), which then resets the 'date of acceptance' to the date FDA receives that information.

3.3 Interaction of the two clocks
- Both clocks start at the same event (receipt). The 15-day acceptance notification falls inside the 120-day period; it does not extend it. FDA's acceptance-review guidance states that once the request is under substantive review 'the calendar days used to conduct the acceptance review (i.e., up to 15 days) are included within the calendar days to reach a final decision for the De Novo request.'
- Therefore, for a complete request with no additional-information submission, the single controlling outer deadline for the order is 120 calendar days from receipt, and the interim deliverable is the acceptance notification at day 15.

====================================================================
4. WHAT THE LIMITS ARE NOT (avoid these substitutions)
====================================================================
- Not MDUFA performance goals. The MDUFA V commitment letter contains FDA performance goals for De Novo requests, but those are non-binding performance commitments, not regulatory limits; they are not the answer to this question and no MDUFA figure is stated in this draft because the specific goal values were not verified against the commitment letter in this pass.
- Not the 30-day Federal Register publication. 21 CFR 860.260(a)(2): 'If FDA grants a De Novo request, within 30 days after the issuance of an order granting the De Novo request, FDA will publish in the Federal Register a notice of the classification order, including any special controls.' This is a post-order publication obligation; it does not enlarge the 120-day order deadline.
- Not the reclassification-petition timelines in Part 860 Subpart C (e.g., 30/60/90/180/210-day figures appearing at 860.130/860.132). Those govern reclassification petitions, not De Novo requests.
- Not a business-day count. Part 860 uses 'days'; FDA's guidance resolves the point as calendar days.

====================================================================
5. CLOCK-EVENT TABLE (what tolls, resets or terminates; none triggered in this scenario)
====================================================================
| Event | Provision | Effect on the 120-day order clock | Triggered here? |
|---|---|---|---|
| FDA refuses to accept; requester supplies corrective information | 860.230(c)(3) | 'Date of acceptance' becomes the date FDA receives the additional information; 860.240(a) restarts 120 days from that receipt | No (accepted at intake) |
| FDA requests additional information during substantive review | 860.240(b)(1) | The regulation does not, by its terms, extend the 120-day period; only a submission that results in acceptance under 860.230 restarts it. Treat any FDA statement that a response 'resets' the clock as a practice/commitment matter to be confirmed in writing | No |
| Requester fails to provide a complete response to an additional-information request within 180 days | 860.250(a)(1) | Request considered withdrawn; review ends | No |
| Requester fails to provide a complete response to RTA deficiencies within 180 days of notification | 860.250(a)(2) | Request considered withdrawn; review ends | No |
| Requester refuses facility inspection under 860.240(c) | 860.250(a)(3) | Request considered withdrawn | No |
| Requester submits written notice of withdrawal | 860.250(a)(4) | Request withdrawn; Agency notifies requester under 860.250(b) | No |

====================================================================
6. WORKED DATE CALCULATION (calendar days; illustration only)
====================================================================
Assume FDA receives the request on 2026-11-02 (day 0 = receipt date; counting forward as calendar days).
- Acceptance notification due no later than 2026-11-02 + 15 days = 2026-11-17.
- Order granting or declining due no later than 2026-11-02 + 120 days:
  - to 2026-11-30 = 28 days (cumulative 28)
  - to 2026-12-31 = 31 days (cumulative 59)
  - to 2027-01-31 = 31 days (cumulative 90)
  - to 2027-02-28 = 28 days (cumulative 118)
  - 2027-03-01 = 119; 2027-03-02 = 120 → due date 2027-03-02.
- Consistency check: the day-15 notification (2026-11-17) precedes the day-120 order date (2027-03-02), as required by the 15-inside-120 structure; no figure in this draft exceeds the 120-day bound.
- If the 120th day falls on a weekend or Federal holiday, the regulation does not itself provide for extension; any relief would come from general FDA practice or a specific commitment, and should be confirmed with FDA in writing rather than assumed.

====================================================================
7. STATEMENT FOR THE REVIEWER TO SIGN OFF
====================================================================
'Under 21 CFR Part 860 as in force on 2026-11-21, where FDA receives a De Novo classification request that is accepted without any additional-information submission: (1) FDA must notify the requester whether the request has been accepted within 15 days after FDA receives the request (21 CFR 860.230(a)); if FDA does not complete the acceptance review within that period, FDA must accept the request and notify the requester (21 CFR 860.230(b)); and (2) FDA must review the request and send an order granting it under 21 CFR 860.260(a) or declining it under 21 CFR 860.260(b) within 120 days after receipt of the request (21 CFR 860.240(a)). The acceptance-review period is included within the 120-day period, so the outside limit for the order is 120 days from receipt. All periods are counted in calendar days.'

====================================================================
8. OPEN ITEMS FOR THE REVIEWER (not blocking the answer)
====================================================================
1. Re-pull 860.230 and 860.240 from a date-specific eCFR point-in-time view fixed at 2026-11-21 to close the two-day capture gap described in section 2.
2. If the requester also wants the non-binding MDUFA V performance goal for De Novo requests, obtain the commitment letter and cite it with its version date; do not substitute it for the 15/120-day limits.
3. If the actual submission was refused acceptance at any point, re-run section 5 — the 120-day clock would then start from receipt of the corrective information under 860.230(c)(3).

====================================================================
9. REFERENCES (full)
====================================================================
1. 21 CFR 860.230, 'Accepting a De Novo request' (paragraphs (a), (b), (c)(1)-(3)). eCFR, Title 21, Part 860, as fetched 2026-11-23T04:25:13Z.
2. 21 CFR 860.240, 'Procedures for review of a De Novo request' (paragraph (a); amendment history '[86 FR 54847, Oct. 5, 2021, as amended at 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025]'). eCFR, Title 21, Part 860, as fetched 2026-11-23T04:25:13Z.
3. 21 CFR 860.250, 'Withdrawal of a De Novo request' (paragraphs (a)(1)-(4), (b)).
4. 21 CFR 860.260, 'Granting or declining a De Novo request' (paragraphs (a)(1), (a)(2), (b)).
5. 21 CFR 860.200, 'Purpose and applicability' (paragraph (b)(1)-(2)).
6. U.S. Code of Federal Regulations, Title 21, Volume 8, Part 860, Subpart D (2025 edition), GovInfo XML, fetched 2026-11-23T04:25:12Z — corroborating text for 860.230(a)/(b) and 860.240(a).
7. FDA guidance document on acceptance review of De Novo classification requests, hosted at https://www.fda.gov/media/152657/download, fetched 2026-11-23T04:25:13Z — states the acceptance review 'should be conducted and completed within 15 calendar days of FDA receiving the De Novo request' and that acceptance-review days 'are included within the calendar days to reach a final decision for the De Novo request'; contains the 'Acceptance Checklist for De Novo Classification Requests'. (Document title/issue date not independently confirmed in this pass; cite the document by its URL and confirm the edition before external use.)
8. Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, section 513(f)(2) — statutory basis for the De Novo pathway, as referenced in 860.200 and 860.230(c)(1)(ii); the statute's own text was not independently verified in this pass and no statutory day figure is asserted here.

verdict.summary:
# ICH E2A seven-day expedited reporting: outer notification limit and follow-up deadline

**Status: draft for review by a qualified clinician / regulatory affairs professional. Not medical advice. Not for patient care.**

---

## 1. Answers

**Ask 1 — outer limit for notifying regulatory agencies.**

> **7 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that the case qualifies (i.e. on or before day 7, with day 0 = the date of first knowledge).**

Unit: calendar days. The notification is to be made *as soon as possible*; 7 calendar days is the outer limit, not a target. Permitted channels per the guideline text are "e.g., by telephone, facsimile transmission, or in writing".

**Ask 2 — follow-up report "as complete as possible" if the full 7-day period is used.**

> **Day 15 measured from day 0** (7 calendar days for the initial notification + 8 additional calendar days = 15 calendar days from day 0).

Unit: calendar days. Arithmetic: 7 + 8 = 15. If the initial notification is sent on day 7, the follow-up is due by day 15; day 15 is also the total elapsed window from day 0 (day 0 + 15 calendar days).

---

## 2. Governing text, quoted in full with source and version

**Source:** ICH Harmonised Tripartite Guideline, *Clinical Safety Data Management: Definitions and Standards for Expedited Reporting*, ICH topic E2A, Step 4 (recommended for adoption 27 October 1994); EU adoption reference **CPMP/ICH/377/95**, legal effective date **1 June 1995** (European Medicines Agency scientific-guideline page, first published 1 June 1995). Full text consulted as hosted by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (URL and retrieval date in §10).

**Operative passage (E2A §3.2 "Reporting Time Frames", numbered item 1 — fatal or life-threatening, unexpected ADRs occurring in clinical investigations):**

> "Regulatory agencies should be notified (e.g., by telephone, facsimile transmission, or in writing) as soon as possible but no later than 7 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that a case qualifies, followed by as complete a report as possible within 8 additional calendar days. This report should include an assessment of the importance and implication of the findings, including relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products."

**Contrasting passage (E2A §3.2, numbered item 2 — all other serious, unexpected ADRs):**

> "Serious, unexpected reactions (ADRs) that are not fatal or life-threatening must be filed as soon as possible but no later than 15 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that the case meets the minimum criteria for expedited reporting."

**Minimum criteria (E2A §3.2, numbered item 3):**

> "...initial reports should be submitted within the prescribed time as long as the following minimum criteria are met: an identifiable patient; a suspect medicinal product; an identifiable reporting source; and an event or outcome that can be identified as serious and unexpected, and for which, in clinical investigation cases, there is [a reasonable possibility that the event was caused by the medicinal product]."

*Note on the quotation:* the fetched passage terminates at "there is"; the bracketed completion is the standard continuation of the E2A sentence and should be checked against the printed guideline before the draft is finalised. The four listed minimum criteria themselves are quoted verbatim.

---

## 3. Population and case qualification (the answers only apply to this population)

| Element | Specification |
|---|---|
| Product status | Investigational (pre-approval) — E2A is expressly the investigational-phase standard; its scope statement notes that premarketing and post-marketing concepts are "interdependent" |
| Reaction | Fatal **or** life-threatening, unexpected adverse drug reaction |
| Causality | Suspected — in clinical investigation cases, a reasonable possibility that the event was caused by the medicinal product |
| Minimum data | Identifiable patient; suspect medicinal product; identifiable reporting source; event identifiable as serious and unexpected |
| Clock start | First knowledge by the sponsor that the case qualifies |

The 7 + 8 day structure in ask 1 applies **only** to the fatal/life-threatening unexpected category. A serious, unexpected ADR that is *not* fatal or life-threatening falls under item 2 and has a single 15-calendar-day outer limit with no 7-day first step. Both routes land on day 15, which is a useful internal consistency check on the arithmetic in §1.

---

## 4. Day counting and the day-0 convention

- **Day 0** = the calendar date on which the sponsor first has knowledge that the case qualifies (i.e. the date the minimum criteria are met). Day 0 is **not** counted as day 1; the count of 7 begins the following calendar day.
- **Calendar days**, not business days: weekends and public holidays do not extend either deadline.
- The E2A text as fetched specifies "calendar days after first knowledge" but does not itself spell out the day-0 convention. The explicit convention is stated in the ICH **E2D** text consulted: *"The regulatory reporting time clock (in calendar days) starts on the date when any personnel of the MAH first receive a case report that fulfills minimum criteria as well as the criteria for expedited reporting. In general, this date should be considered as day 0."* (ICH E2D, §3.2.2 "Time Clock Start Point"; document footer "E2D ver3.8 (2003JUL18)", distributed on the FDA guidance site as a **draft** — January 2025 update. Because this is a draft, the day-0 convention is stated here as the operative sponsor convention, not as final E2A text.)
- Note also from the same E2D draft, §3.2.2: *"When additional medically significant information is received for a previously reported case, the regulatory reporting time clock begins again for submission of the follow-up report."* This is a separate trigger from the 8-additional-day rule and does not change the day-15 answer; it can make a follow-up due earlier if significant new information arrives sooner.
- **Conservative reading applied here:** the 8 additional days run from the end of the 7-day window (day 0 + 15), not from the actual date the initial notification was transmitted. A sponsor that notifies on day 2 should not plan on a day-10 follow-up; plan to day 15.

---

## 5. Worked timeline (all figures in calendar days from day 0)

| # | Milestone | Day from day 0 | Example (day 0 = Mon 3 Mar 2025) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | First knowledge; minimum criteria met; clock starts | 0 | Mon 3 Mar 2025 |
| 2 | Initial notification to regulatory agencies — outer limit | **7** | Mon 10 Mar 2025 |
| 3 | Follow-up report "as complete as possible" — outer limit | **15** | Tue 18 Mar 2025 |

Arithmetic verification: 3 Mar 2025 + 7 days = 10 Mar 2025; 10 Mar 2025 + 8 days = 18 Mar 2025; 3 Mar 2025 + 15 days = 18 Mar 2025. The two routes to the follow-up date agree. No weekend or holiday adjustment is applied to either date.

---

## 6. What the initial notification and the follow-up must contain

E2A is explicit that the initial report may be sent on minimum criteria alone: *"Information for final description and evaluation of a case report may not be available within the required time frames for reporting outlined above. Nevertheless, for regulatory purposes, initial reports should be submitted within the prescribed time as long as the following minimum criteria are met..."*

On format, E2A states: *"The CIOMS-I form has been a widely accepted standard for expedited adverse event reporting. However, no matter what the form or format used, it is important that certain basic information/data elements, when available, be included with any expedited report, whether in a tabular or narrative presentation."* The administrative/sponsor elements E2A lists include, verbatim:

> "Source of report: Was it spontaneous, from a clinical investigation (provide details), from the literature (provide copy), other?
> Date event report was first received by sponsor/manufacturer,
> Country in which event occurred,
> Type of report filed to authorities: initial or follow-up (first, second, etc.),
> Name and address of sponsor/manufacturer/company,
> Name, address, telephone number, and FAX number of contact person in reporting company or institution,
> Identifying regulatory code or number for marketing authorization dossier or clinical investigation process for the suspected product (for example IND or CTX number, NDA number),
> Sponsor/manufacturer's identification number for the case (This number should be the same for the initial and follow-up reports on the same case)."

Operational consequence: the initial 7-day notification is a valid, complete submission if it carries the four minimum criteria plus the administrative block above, and the follow-up submitted by day 15 must carry the full case (narrative, event details, reporter details, sponsor assessment of importance and implication, relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products). Use the identical sponsor case identification number on both, and label the second submission as a follow-up.

---

## 7. Jurisdictional overrides that must be checked before the draft is used

The 7/15 answers above are the **ICH E2A** answers. They are not automatically the operative legal deadlines in every region, and the following must be resolved for the specific case:

- **United States.** The FDA-hosted E2A text carries an explicit caveat, quoted verbatim: *"The time frames and definitions in this guideline differ from those in the Code of Federal Regulations [21 CFR 314.80]. Until the regulations are revised, the time frames and definitions in the CFR should be followed."* For a US-marketed product the CFR governs; for an IND safety report the applicable provision is 21 CFR 312.32. Paragraph-level citations to 21 CFR 314.80(c)(1) and 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1) are given for orientation only and **must be re-verified against the current eCFR text** before use; the numeric answers in §1 rest on the E2A passages quoted in §2, not on the CFR.
- **European Union.** E2A is adopted in the EU as CPMP/ICH/377/95 (legal effective date 1 June 1995). For interventional clinical trials conducted under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014, SUSAR reporting time frames are set by that Regulation (Article 42) and its implementing acts; those provisions should be checked and cited at article level from the current consolidated text before this draft is finalised.
- **Other regions.** National implementing guidance (e.g. gateway, portal or paper channel, local follow-up rules, local language requirements) has not been retrieved and is not cited here. If the case falls in such a region, that guidance must be added to this draft before use.
- **Whether the case is investigational or marketed.** E2A is the investigational-phase standard. For a marketed product, the post-approval framework (and, in the US, the CFR as noted above) may impose different or additional obligations.

None of these overrides changes the E2A figures of 7 and 15; they determine whether the E2A figures are the ones that legally bind this particular case.

---

## 8. Audit documentation the sponsor should hold for this case

1. Evidence of the **day-0 determination**: the source document (e.g. initial notification from the site), the date and time it was first received by any sponsor personnel, and the identity of the recipient.
2. A signed statement that the four minimum criteria were met on that date, with the elements enumerated.
3. The **day-7** and **day-15** due dates calculated and recorded at the time of triage (not reconstructed later), using calendar-day arithmetic with day 0 excluded.
4. Transmission records: gateway/portal acknowledgement or fax/telephone record, with date and time, and the case identification number used on both submissions.
5. A record of any medically significant follow-up information received after the initial report and the re-started clock it triggers (E2D draft §3.2.2).

---

## 9. Limits of this draft

- The answers are stated for the population in §3 and the E2A framework; §7 lists the checks required before they can be relied on for a specific case.
- The day-0 counting convention is sourced to a **draft** ICH E2D text; confirm against the final E2D guideline and against local guidance.
- The truncation in the quoted minimum-criteria sentence and the paragraph-level CFR citations are flagged above and require verification against the printed guideline and the current eCFR.
- This document is a regulatory-evidence draft for a qualified clinician and regulatory affairs lead to review and sign off. It is not medical advice and is not for patient care.

verdict.summary: IND submission serial-numbering question; a wrong answer is a reversible regulatory documentation error rather than directly harmful.

asks.quote: What three-digit serial number must the next submission carry?

verdict.summary:
Answer: 018.

Basis and calculation: Under the IND serial-numbering convention reflected in Form FDA 1571 and 21 CFR Part 312, the initial IND is assigned serial number 000. Each subsequent submission to that IND receives the next sequential serial number. Submissions under 21 CFR 312.30 (protocol amendments), 21 CFR 312.31 (information amendments), 21 CFR 312.32 (IND safety reports) and 21 CFR 312.33 (annual reports) are submissions to the same IND and participate in the same serial sequence. Given the stated premise that the initial IND and 17 later submissions are all correctly numbered, the 17 later submissions occupy serial numbers 001 through 017 inclusive: 001, 002, ..., 017. The next submission therefore carries 017 + 1 = 018. It must be rendered as a three-digit serial number with zero-padding: 018, not 18 and not 0018. It should appear in the Form FDA 1571 Serial Number field and in the cover letter.

Sources/versions named: 21 CFR Part 312 (eCFR text as supplied/current), including 21 CFR 312.23 (IND content and format), 312.30, 312.31, 312.32 and 312.33; Form FDA 1571 Serial Number field and instructions.

Assumptions accepted from the request: initial IND = serial 000; all 17 later submissions were serial-numbered consecutively with no gaps, duplications, withdrawals or voided numbers; three-digit zero-padded format applies. If any of those premises is false, the number must be recomputed from the actual submission history. This is a draft for a qualified regulatory/clinical reviewer and is not medical advice.

quotes.whole:
§ 807.81 When a premarket notification submission is required.




(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria:




(1) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time; that is, the device is not of the same type as, or is not substantially equivalent to, 



(i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or 





(ii) a device introduced for commercial distribution after May 28, 1976, that has subsequently been reclassified into class I or II.








(2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section.






(3) The device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use. The following constitute significant changes or modifications that require a premarket notification:




(i) A change or modification in the device that could significantly affect the safety or effectiveness of the device, e.g., a significant change or modification in design, material, chemical composition, energy source, or manufacturing process.






(ii) A major change or modification in the intended use of the device.










(b) 




(1) A premarket notification under this subpart is not required for a device for which:




(i) A premarket approval application under section 515 of the act, or for which a petition to reclassify under section 513(f)(2) of the act, is pending before the Food and Drug Administration, or






(ii) There is a predetermined change control plan (PCCP) cleared under section 515C of the act, provided that the change is consistent with the PCCP.








(2) The appropriate FDA Center Director may determine that the submission and grant of a written request for an exception or alternative under § 801.128 or § 809.11 of this chapter satisfies the requirement in paragraph (a)(3) of this section.







(c) In addition to complying with the requirements of this part, owners or operators of device establishments that manufacture radiation-emitting electronic products, as defined in § 1000.3 of this chapter, shall comply with the reporting requirements of part 1002 of this chapter.

§ 807.85 Exemption from premarket notification.
(a) A custom device is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

§ 807.85 Exemption from premarket notification.




(a) A custom device is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.




(1) It is intended for use by a patient named in the order of the physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person); or






(2) It is intended solely for use by a physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person) and is not generally available to, or generally used by, other physicians or dentists (or other specially qualified persons).
quotes.whole:
§ 807.85 Exemption from premarket notification.




(a) A custom device is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.




(1) It is intended for use by a patient named in the order of the physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person); or

quotes.whole:
Subpart E—Premarket Notification Procedures
§ 807.81
When a premarket notification submission is required.
(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria:
(1) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time; that is, the device is not of the same type as, or is not substantially equivalent to, (i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or (ii) a device introduced for commercial distribution after May 28, 1976, that has subsequently been reclassified into class I or II.
(2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section.

verdict.summary:
# Regulatory analysis: premarket notification obligation for a device within the meaning of FD&C Act §520(b), under 21 CFR Part 807 Subpart E as in force on 2026-11-21

**Status:** Draft regulatory analysis for review by a qualified regulatory professional. Not legal advice. Not for use in patient care.

---

## 1. Question presented and answer

**Question (ask 2).** A device meets the custom-device meaning in section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act), 21 U.S.C. 360j(b). Under 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E, as in force on 2026-11-21, must its manufacturer submit a premarket notification at least 90 days before commercial distribution?

**Answer: No.** 21 CFR 807.85(a) states, in terms: "A custom device is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act." Section 807.85 sits inside Subpart E, the same subpart that contains the 90-day rule in §807.81(a). A device that is within the meaning of §520(b) is therefore outside the class of devices for which §807.81(a) requires a premarket notification, and the 90-day advance-submission obligation in §807.81(a) does not attach to it.

**The answer is conditional, and the condition is substantive, not clerical.** The exemption in §807.85(a) is keyed to the device being "within the meaning of section 520(b)." If the device does not in fact satisfy every element of §520(b), or if it loses the exemption because a §520(b)(2) condition is not met, then §807.81(a) applies in full and the manufacturer **must** submit a premarket notification at least **90 days** before it proposes to begin introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution. The conditions that preserve and that defeat the exemption are set out in §5 below, with units.

---
